items.title: I analyzed 10,000+ buyside analyst reports from top hedge funds: - Found 7 things that separate great stock pitches …
items.snippet: I analyzed 10,000+ buyside analyst reports from top hedge funds: - Found 7 things that separate great stock pitches from mediocre ones -- also something I consistently see missing from new analyst…
items.content_text: [1/14 @MapleLeafCap] I analyzed 10,000+ buyside analyst reports from top hedge funds: - Found 7 things that separate great stock pitches from mediocre ones -- also something I consistently see missing from new analysts; - Only ~20% of buyside analysts do all of them consistently; - Retail investors? Almost none (lol) A thread 🧵: --- [2/14 @MapleLeafCap] What surprised me: The best pitches were often longer - but every word earned its place -- They didn't have "better access" (ok maybe sometimes) - they just asked better questions and proved their answers Result? Higher conviction, longer read-time, better returns. --- [3/14 @MapleLeafCap] 1/ Thesis conviction in the first paragraph Great pitches: 100% state their thesis definitively in the first 3 sentences Mediocre pitches: 67% contain hedging language like "tell me what I'm missing" The best analysts don't ask for permission. They state what they believe and why. --- [4/14 @MapleLeafCap] 2/ A clearly stated variant view Every great pitch answers: "What does the market believe, and why is it wrong?" Not "this is undervalued" - that's a conclusion, not an edge "Consensus thinks margins peak at 15%, but my channel checks show 22% is sustainable because..." - that's a variant view. --- [5/14 @MapleLeafCap] 3/ Proprietary primary research "3 former execs told me the product pipeline is stronger than reported" "Top 3 customers confirmed they're increasing spend 40%" "A competitor's sales rep said they're losing deals to this company" You can't find this in 10-Ks. The best pitches prove their edge with sources. --- [6/14 @MapleLeafCap] 4/ Scenario analysis that tells a story Not just bull/base/bear with numbers in a table The best pitches walk you through each world: "In the bull case, AWS reprices and margins expand to X because Y happens... here's exactly what that looks like..." Assumptions explicit. Logic clear. You can follow the math. --- [7/14 @MapleLeafCap] 5/ Specific risks with kill conditions Mediocre: "competition could increase" Elite: "if AWS cuts prices 20%, margins compress to X% - I exit at $Y" The best analysts define exactly what would prove them wrong. No ego. Just process. --- [8/14 @MapleLeafCap] 6/ No background padding Mediocre pitches: 2 pages of company history before the thesis Great pitches: just enough context for the decision - nothing more Background is what weak analysts hide behind. Your reader is busy. Respect their time. --- [9/14 @MapleLeafCap] 7/ Explicit downside floor with asymmetric framing The best pitches quantify both sides: "$2 of downside, $20+ of upside" "If I'm wrong, I lose 15%. If I'm right, I 3x." This isn't confidence theater - it's showing you did the work on the downside too. --- [10/14 @MapleLeafCap] The pattern? Great pitches are decision-ready. They give you: - Why the market is wrong (variant view) - Proprietary evidence backing it - Scenarios that tell a story, not just numbers - What would change their mind (kill conditions) - Only what matters Everything else is noise. --- [11/14 @MapleLeafCap] So I built an AI that writes pitches this way. 6 AI analysts with different investing philosophies debate each other across 5 rounds A research director challenges every assumption The output: institutional-quality memos in 30 minutes See examples: http://tickertothesis.com --- [12/14 @MapleLeafCap] Here are a few examples: --- [13/14 @MapleLeafCap] Want to try it yourself? I packaged the whole system as a downloadable skill you can run locally Go to http://bidclub.ai (@bidclubai) and grab it: https://www.bidclub.ai/post/eefb6740-2a94-4a0e-9149-17fa70f76d32 Generate your own buyside-quality research on any ticker --- [14/14 @MapleLeafCap] tl;dr - after analyzing 10,000+ analyst reports: 1. Lead with conviction 2. Prove your variant view 3. Cite proprietary sources 4. Tell stories with scenarios 5. Define your kill conditions 6. Cut the fluff 7. Show asymmetric payoff The market rewards clarity.

items.title: This news article is absolutely insane and probably a good glimpse into what the future of hedge funds look like in a…
items.snippet: This news article is absolutely insane and probably a good glimpse into what the future of hedge funds look like in an AI driven world Coatue backed hedge fund, Epicenter, is using AI to replace …
items.content_text: [1/25 @BoringBiz_] This news article is absolutely insane and probably a good glimpse into what the future of hedge funds look like in an AI driven world Coatue backed hedge fund, Epicenter, is using AI to replace massive teams of hedge fund analysts Their AI bot, Eve, is plugged into every part of the firm, including emails and every trade that the fund puts on Without any prompts, the AI bot is able to assign tasks to human analysts and write code on their behalf Eve also contains a screening tool which scours through more than 13,000 company disclosures, listens to podcasts, and summarizes news reports on specific businesses The AI bot can then generate primers and custom podcasts on behalf of the human analysts without requiring any instructions beforehand If you read this and don’t think that AI is going to impact headcount in finance, you are absolutely mistaken --- [2/25 @chikaibeh_1] @BoringBiz_ @grok how do they write article on X? --- [3/25 @Time7MDI] @BoringBiz_ zero reason for human intellect in 3 years in business due to ai. watch and see. the math checks out. --- [4/25 @atomicrabits] @BoringBiz_ Soon we will be forced to develop AI Antidotes. Its getting out of our hands real quick, massive global slavery loading? --- [5/25 @cc_video_edit] @BoringBiz_ Feels like leverage more than a full replacement right now. --- [6/25 @aanalystbro] @BoringBiz_ I guarantee you this fund will do horribly and be shut down. Coatue has a *really* bad track record doing these types of experiments. --- [7/25 @ScroogeCap] @BoringBiz_ They tryna be RenTech or what --- [8/25 @rcwillenbrock] @BoringBiz_ is eve changing how decisions get made or just making the existing process faster & cheaper --- [9/25 @chisaehawng] @BoringBiz_ curious how eve handles black swan events that arent in training data --- [10/25 @Joseph_Paul_V] @BoringBiz_ AI can analyze written and recorded documents, but in the situation where everyone has access to an AI this does not generate value only savings, as you correctly noted. AI fails to have a grasp on the material world at this time; the most important domain for humans. --- [11/25 @uv] @BoringBiz_ they should hit us up --- [12/25 @BullBrezza] @BoringBiz_ Sharp take - but here’s a tighter, punchy reply in your tone: Everyone sees efficiency. Few see fragility. You replaced analysts with answers… now nobody knows how to ask questions. When the model breaks, there’s no human left to fix it-only prompts feeding a black box.” --- [13/25 @lucacs] @BoringBiz_ we're all just doing the same shit aren't we https://t.co/irbtIlPW9k --- [14/25 @thecleverrat] @BoringBiz_ Eh humans will always exist in investing. Ai bots trying to put invest other AI bots are similar to humans vs humans imo. --- [15/25 @CashflowingOptn] @BoringBiz_ No shit this should’ve been done in hedge funds --- [16/25 @DannyOConnell47] @BoringBiz_ No serious investor is using “podcasts” as the delivery method for research info. --- [17/25 @HochstatMichael] @BoringBiz_ Shrink add enjois linkedin --- [18/25 @AdiFlips] @BoringBiz_ does this actually generate better returns, or just cheaper headcount? Those aren't the same thing. --- [19/25 @bob674971282334] @BoringBiz_ Fundamental hedge funds are a joke anyways, no serious quant fund is doing this shit. --- [20/25 @tonitrades_] @BoringBiz_ Heard the same thing about quant funds in 2010. They still needed humans when markets got weird. AI reads patterns fine, but who built those patterns in the first place? --- [21/25 @imjszhang] @BoringBiz_ Eve can crunch data. Eve can't get fired. Hedge funds don't pay for intelligence—they pay for accountability when bets go wrong. AI replaces labor. It doesn't replace responsibility. --- [22/25 @StrCashHomie] @BoringBiz_ This is the future of marketing by hedge funds. --- [23/25 @jcantwit] @BoringBiz_ Global Alpha 2.0 --- [24/25 @EshelGeffen] @BoringBiz_ Assign what tasks to human analysts? Whats left to do? It sounds like those at risk are the senior guys who delegate and distribute work. Plus the presence of such bs alone would make any analyst and PM question themselves & would distort their own thought process. Net -ve. --- [25/25 @codymclain] @BoringBiz_ what's wild is they're not just replacing junior analysts, they're going after the whole research pipeline. most funds still think AI is just for backtesting

items.title: The question of whether AI will generate alpha in the investment process to me is rather obvious. AI can help us: 1…
items.snippet: The question of whether AI will generate alpha in the investment process to me is rather obvious. AI can help us: 1) know companies better 2) track them more closely 3) make better decisions Use…
items.content_text: [1/11 @FundamentEdge] The question of whether AI will generate alpha in the investment process to me is rather obvious. AI can help us: 1) know companies better 2) track them more closely 3) make better decisions Used effectively, agentic AI is clearly a powerful tool for alpha generation. But it's the system around AI that matters. AI doesn't know the answers to my questions, but can enable a process around building much more comprehensive insight in the same block of time. Don't outsource, augment. Like any tool, however, how you use the tool is what matters. I'll give an example. I like to time-block parts of the investment process in my pedagogical approach. How investors spend their time is a critical decision when we all are working with the same ~3,000 hours in a year. I could map out a 300 hour due diligence process on a name, but then I only get 10 shots on goal in a year. If you've been in the seat of a public investor, you know this is a never ending game of triage, particularly as coverage broadens & idea velocity demands increase. When thinking about time blocking your investment process with AI, I would encourage you to do a "before & after" approach. I hear from investors often "I did the AI augmented approach, but I don't feel like I know the name as well". I sympathize with that, and agree, but when I push back the obvious point is that they tried to compress 60 hours down to 20 hours. There certainly will be comprehension lost in translation trying to do that. My suggestion is to time block that entire 60 hours. You are saving ~40 hours, how will you redeploy that 40 hours? Your portfolio won't magically include 3x the number of ideas, so how do you increase the research quality of the existing idea flow? This is where I think top decile investment process will radically change in the next 9-18 months. AI will raise the floor in investment process quality, democratizing "institutional like" quality, but raising the ceiling is what matters: alpha is an adaptive game where power law prevails. Running the same desktop research game with small snippets of primary research won't continue to work, in my opinion. Raising the ceiling, to me, is not about working fewer hours, it's about driving much more comprehensive understanding of the business & the stock in that same 60 hours. Some of this is "what's old is new again" (i.e. for example, multi-manager investment professionals are less present at trade shows than Tiger investors, for example, due to burden of desktop research demands in coverage model). But some of it is thoughtfully deploying brand new AI-augmented processes that can drive deeper comprehension, closer KPI tracking and help drive better, less emotional decision making. To simplify, a compression of desktop research opens up meaningful capacity for more primary research. The critical question then becomes , even if the compression of 60 to 20 leads to some degradation of name comprehension, is that degradation more than offset by the brand new 40 hours of AI augmented primary research. My belief is yes. --- [2/11 @jamesthomason] @FundamentEdge This is such a good take. The models get you ramped to consensus and key drivers in record time. Your alpha is outside the building. The models free you to do the work that actually results in a differentiated view. --- [3/11 @hedgie007] @FundamentEdge If everyone has access, and AI has democratized the process and tool availability, couldn’t you argue the opportunity for alpha generation has been made harder? --- [4/11 @S_Kadakia] @FundamentEdge Agree on the redeployment into primary. Worth underlining how primary research itself is changing. AI can structure and scale expert convos in ways that weren't possible 2 years ago. --- [5/11 @argosyinvestors] @FundamentEdge Only 3,000 hours?! https://t.co/yalXCFtAiw --- [6/11 @ChauHymn48817] @FundamentEdge For someone starting off their career would you say it'd be better to do it without the AI for the first year and then slowly layer in AI-augmentation to save time for primary research? Or would the competitive disadvantage compared to fellow interns be too great --- [7/11 @FundamentEdge] It's such a great question. I think a lot of it depends on the type of seat you're in and the culture and expectations of your managing PM. I bias towards learning the artisanal way in the first 9-18 months with selective AI augmentation mostly around developing more things to read. But I could also make the case for deeper augmentation faster. There are really two sides and very strong views on both --- [8/11 @ThetaCatalyst] @FundamentEdge Well said. Loved the most recent YouTube vid --- [9/11 @jackzumwalt] @FundamentEdge This is actually super helpful to gauge our focus at Kimpton. Up for a call? I think we would get a lot out of your perspective. --- [10/11 @FundamentEdge] @jackzumwalt Yeah happy to chat - DM me --- [11/11 @kwasijouer] @FundamentEdge After the last 5 days I’ve spent being able to utilize Computer to create an exoskeleton system and watching the iterative responses and connections it was outputting in response. I fully agree with this!

AI will raise the floor in investment process quality, democratizing "institutional like" quality, but raising the ceiling is what matters: alpha is an adaptive game where power law prevails. Running the same desktop research game with small snippets of primary research won't continue to work, in my opinion. Raising the ceiling, to me, is not about working fewer hours, it's about driving much more comprehensive understanding of the business & the stock in that same 60 hours. Some of this is "what's old is new again" (i.e. for example, multi-manager investment professionals are less present at trade shows than Tiger investors, for example, due to burden of desktop research demands in coverage model). But some of it is thoughtfully deploying brand new AI-augmented processes that can drive deeper comprehension, closer KPI tracking and help drive better, less emotional decision making. To simplify, a compression of desktop research opens up meaningful capacity for more primary research. The critical question then becomes , even if the compression of 60 to 20 leads to some degradation of name comprehension, is that degradation more than offset by the brand new 40 hours of AI augmented primary research. My belief is yes. --- [2/11 @jamesthomason] @FundamentEdge This is such a good take. The models get you ramped to consensus and key drivers in record time. Your alpha is outside the building. The models free you to do the work that actually results in a differentiated view. --- [3/11 @hedgie007] @FundamentEdge If everyone has access, and AI has democratized the process and tool availability, couldn’t you argue the opportunity for alpha generation has been made harder? --- [4/11 @S_Kadakia] @FundamentEdge Agree on the redeployment into primary. Worth underlining how primary research itself is changing. AI can structure and scale expert convos in ways that weren't possible 2 years ago. --- [5/11 @argosyinvestors] @FundamentEdge Only 3,000 hours?! https://t.co/yalXCFtAiw --- [6/11 @ChauHymn48817] @FundamentEdge For someone starting off their career would you say it'd be better to do it without the AI for the first year and then slowly layer in AI-augmentation to save time for primary research? Or would the competitive disadvantage compared to fellow interns be too great --- [7/11 @FundamentEdge] It's such a great question. I think a lot of it depends on the type of seat you're in and the culture and expectations of your managing PM. I bias towards learning the artisanal way in the first 9-18 months with selective AI augmentation mostly around developing more things to read. But I could also make the case for deeper augmentation faster. There are really two sides and very strong views on both --- [8/11 @ThetaCatalyst] @FundamentEdge Well said. Loved the most recent YouTube vid --- [9/11 @jackzumwalt] @FundamentEdge This is actually super helpful to gauge our focus at Kimpton. Up for a call? I think we would get a lot out of your perspective. --- [10/11 @FundamentEdge] @jackzumwalt Yeah happy to chat - DM me --- [11/11 @kwasijouer] @FundamentEdge After the last 5 days I’ve spent being able to utilize Computer to create an exoskeleton system and watching the iterative responses and connections it was outputting in response. I fully agree with this!

items.content_text: [1/2 @karpathy] Wow, this tweet went very viral! I wanted share a possibly slightly improved version of the tweet in an "idea file". The idea of the idea file is that in this era of LLM agents, there is less of a point/need of sharing the specific code/app, you just share the idea, then the other person's agent customizes & builds it for your specific needs. So here's the idea in a gist format: https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f You can give this to your agent and it can build you your own LLM wiki and guide you on how to use it etc. It's intentionally kept a little bit abstract/vague because there are so many directions to take this in. And ofc, people can adjust the idea or contribute their own in the Discussion which is cool. --- [2/2 @karpathy] Surprised with how good the comments on github gists are. A lot more helpful, insightful, constructive, a lot less AI... Is it the user community? The markdown format? The (lack of) incentives? Suddenly feeling like I should gist more. @github consider competing with X (?)

items.content_text: [1/2 @FundamentEdge] One of many reasons I am so bullish on agents in the investment process is the trajectory of talent building in this space right now. Just one of many examples: Jack Meehan from Nephron (one of if not the top healthcare sell-side firm) leaving to build an AI-native research company in healthcare. Agents are only as capable as the power of their data inputs & workflow orchestration. And the native data (primarily web-scrape) and workflow orchestration (not buy-side native) is quite bad. But as an ecosystem builds around the agent to unlock the "intelligence overhang", I expect agents to improve materially and reach institutional grade. Pay attention to what Jack does next (and many others like him who are betting their careers on building agent-legible inputs) --- [2/2 @EdgeCGroup] @FundamentEdge The difference between the agents that actually win will be data quality.

items.snippet: Andrej Karpathy: "90% of your AI coding bill is paying for context you didn't need to send" Here are 10 things senior AI engineers stopped wasting tokens on: 1. Auto-context loading 50 files for …
items.content_text: [1/37 @DeRonin_] Andrej Karpathy: "90% of your AI coding bill is paying for context you didn't need to send" Here are 10 things senior AI engineers stopped wasting tokens on: 1. Auto-context loading 50 files for a 30-line fix: $1.20/turn for tokens you'll never read. 80% input waste, every session 2. Running Opus on lint, format, and rename tasks: $0.60 for what Haiku nails at $0.02. 30x overpay on the cleanup tier 3. Tool call loops that re-send the full repo on every retry: 5x context cost per agentic flow. fixing these alone cuts 30-50% of bills 4. Sonnet as the default model: Kimi 2.6 matches its quality on most coding tasks at 1/6 the cost. defaulting to Sonnet in 2026 is leaving 60-70% on the table 5. Streaming responses on stable-prefix workflows: kills your prompt cache. you pay 10x for tokens that should have cost cents 6. "Just in case" file includes: 80,000-token prompts that should be 3,000. context bloat is the silent budget killer 7. Per-session knowledge rebuilding: 10 min writing a SKILL.md once vs paying agents to re-figure out your environment every run. $4 vs $0.30 per execution 8. Single-model setups: premium tier on every task is the most expensive mistake in AI coding right now 9. Asking 10 small questions one at a time: 10 separate input prefix charges vs one batched call. 70-90% savings on routine workflows 10. Buying Claude Pro + ChatGPT Plus + Cursor Pro: you seriously use one. the other two are habit, not utility what actually compounds instead: - context discipline (grep before fetching, always) - prompt caching on every stable prefix - multi-model routing (Kimi 2.6 default, Opus for the 10%) - graduated skills via SKILL.md files - profiling tool calls before optimizing prompts - the routing mindset (right model for right task) in 12 months, the gap between developers shipping on $200/month and $4,000/month budgets won't be skill it'll be how well they route study this. --- [2/37 @0xCodez] @DeRonin_ another solid workshop by Andrej Karpathy, thanks for sharing brother ! --- [3/37 @Hiraweb3] @DeRonin_ clean execution beats flashy tools every time --- [4/37 @zhuren1992] @DeRonin_ Context discipline is the new alpha for AI coding budgets. --- [5/37 @MindTheGapMTG] @DeRonin_ Token routing saves 20%. Proper constraint files save 80%. The real cost isn't which model you call, it's your agent burning 50K tokens re-discovering your codebase every session because nobody wrote down the architecture decisions. Fix the memory layer before the router. --- [6/37 @yujin68so] @DeRonin_ Skill docs over session churn every time --- [7/37 @tawer1O] @DeRonin_ Does prompt caching in kimi 2.6 cut costs on repetitive code checks? --- [8/37 @kanukagi] @DeRonin_ コンテクストの無駄遣いはAIコーディングの大きな出費です。新しいアプローチを試してみることが重要です。 --- [9/37 @slatt_eth] @DeRonin_ kimi killing it ngl --- [10/37 @woniu513513] @DeRonin_ 搬个板凳慢慢学 --- [11/37 @EffortlessSteve] @DeRonin_ 90% of your AI coding bill is CI. The other 90% is your time. --- [12/37 @marmot_sh] @DeRonin_ We built marmot in part to offload lower-cognitive work from primary agents to lower cost models and to minimise context bloat https://t.co/7iZIO9Yihp --- [13/37 @leaf_sanren] 谁敢想，这是一年前的视频了都，但都不过时。我翻出来当时的notebook LM笔记，大家共勉： 第一，LLM 不是一个“答案机器”，更像一个随时可调用的思考搭子。 Karpathy 很少把它当成一次性问答工具，而是不断让它解释、改写、对比、补全、生成候选方案，再由自己判断。这里的关键不是“让 AI 替你思考”，而是让它扩大你的思考带宽。 第二，很多人只关心 prompt，但他其实更重视 context。 同一个问题，你给不给背景、文件、约束、目标，结果完全不是一个东西。尤其是长文、代码、论文、文档类任务，真正重要的不是一句神奇提示词，而是你有没有把材料、标准和边界讲清楚。 第三，他用 LLM 的方式很“分层”。 简单问题直接问；需要事实的任务结合搜索；需要处理材料的任务上传文件；需要执行的任务交给代码工具；需要长期复用的任务再沉淀成固定流程。 这点挺重要的，因为很多人一上来就想找“最强模型”，但其实应该先判断任务属于哪一层。 第四，代码场景里，他不是让 AI 一口气“帮我做完整项目”。 更像是：先让 AI 读代码、解释结构、定位相关文件、提出修改方案，然后小步实现，再看 diff、跑测试、继续修。 这其实不像 prompt 技巧，更像工程管理。AI 写代码越强，人越需要会拆任务、会验收、会控制风险。 第五，他对 LLM 的态度并不迷信。 视频里很多地方能感觉到，他会频繁 cross-check，会让模型给多个版本，会自己保留最终判断。 这可能是普通用户和高手最大的区别：普通人拿 AI 输出当答案，高手拿 AI 输出当候选材料。 很多人还在把 LLM 当聊天框用，问一句，等一句。 但 Karpathy 展示的是另一种用法：把 LLM 当成一个可以参与搜索、阅读、写作、编码、学习和创作的通用工作界面。 真正值得学的不是“他用了哪些产品”，而是这套习惯： 给足上下文， 拆小任务， 让模型生成多个候选， 自己做判断， 再把高频任务沉淀成流程。 这可能也是现在普通 AI 用户和高级 AI 用户最明显的分水岭。 不是谁背了更多 prompt，而是谁更会把自己的判断、材料和工作流组织起来。 --- [14/37 @abxxai] @DeRonin_ prompt caching getting killed by streaming is a sneaky one --- [15/37 @realtechodyssey] @DeRonin_ The cost problem is really a runtime design problem...uncontrolled context, repeated discovery, weak caching, and no model routing policy compound quickly. --- [16/37 @manojvasi7777] @DeRonin_ Built TokenTelemetry for @OpenAI, @AnthropicAI, @GoogleAI, @cursor_ai & Copilot workflows. Track tokens, costs & sessions locally. Open source: https://t.co/7sQSg679Os --- [17/37 @datagobes] @DeRonin_ Great stuff. I didn’t know about the streaming responses ruining cache. How does streaming responses ruin the prompt cache? --- [18/37 @_mauriciorubio] @DeRonin_ This is an extremely long way of saying you should switch to and only use Codex --- [19/37 @DmitriiBuchilin] @DeRonin_ You can try my library to cut the context and control children spawning https://t.co/roVCs2nfpl --- [20/37 @Gaurav_vij137] @DeRonin_ @Shen19589425 You should checkout Neo AI engineer. It can autonomously audit and optimize AI pipelines. Here’s a case study of how it optimized a RAG chat agent to reduce cost by 79%: https://t.co/YvaQROFClL --- [21/37 @deus_machinea] @DeRonin_ An opensource project using LLMs to analyze code and create index. https://t.co/u4bLg25Bf5 Their benchmark shows 40% more accuracy on Monorepos on swebench-pro and 30% more accuracy on cross-repo, while saving 70% costs. --- [22/37 @laniakea001] @DeRonin_ 1/7 Karpathy这句"AI编程90%的Token都浪费了"，听着就让人虎躯一震！我之前也觉得AI写代码效率超高，现在看来，原来是这90%的"虚高"。 --- [23/37 @laniakea001] @DeRonin_ 1/7 Karpathy这句"AI编程90%的Token都浪费了"，听着就让人虎躯一震！我之前也觉得AI写代码效率超高，现在看来，原来是这90%的"虚高" --- [24/37 @YotamBlu] @DeRonin_ man, this hits. i've been dumping entire garmin api docs into claude when i just need the auth endpoint. the token tax is real and it's silent. the trick is knowing exactly what context actually matters before you hit send. --- [25/37 @Larrywilsonn_] @DeRonin_ Dumping your whole project into the most expensive AI just to fix one line of code does not make you a genius engineer. it just makes you the perfect customer to pay a massive API bill. --- [26/37 @gerardsans] @DeRonin_ https://t.co/E28cBAnfOn --- [27/37 @vganesh] @DeRonin_ how about using kiro instead. --- [28/37 @priyankarocks] Spot on—the routing mindset is table stakes now. One tactic that’s quietly compounding for me: dynamic context versioning. Instead of static SKILL.md or full greps, I maintain tiny “diff snapshots” (think: git-style summaries of the last N changes to key modules). Before a task, the agent first pulls only the delta relevant to the ticket (via a simple embedding index on commit messages + changed files). For a refactor in auth flow, it loads the 400-token summary of “what changed since last stable version” instead of 20k tokens of current code + history. Now wht if we treated agent sessions like git branches? Fork a lightweight context branch per feature, merge insights back to main memory layer on success, and let agents “rebase” cheaply on conflicts?!? No more per-session rediscovery, and you get audit trails for free. --- [29/37 @ChUd94747] @DeRonin_ Complete nonsense. I use Opus with full context and a €140/mo Ultra sub. I rarely hit the 5-hour limit, and the only real risk is a model error. Always use the best model with maximum context for the best results. --- [30/37 @aadhilkh] @DeRonin_ You are basically telling the vibe coders to learn coding! Nice. --- [31/37 @britanianec] @DeRonin_ 毎月の予算の違いは、スキルではなく、どれくらいうまくルーティングできるかになるでしょう。研究してください。 --- [32/37 @geren8te] @DeRonin_ yep. most teams are paying premium model prices to shovel boilerplate. better skill boundaries save more than prompt tricks. building https://t.co/wAXM9FxxVe for that layer. --- [33/37 @mihirchoudhary] @DeRonin_ Would love to get your thoughts on https://t.co/QEPjZQXrF4 --- [34/37 @asukahaox] @DeRonin_ コーディングの代金の90％は送信しなくてもよかった文脈に支払われています。高齢AIエンジニアが無駄なトークンを使わなくなった10のポイントについての返信です。 --- [35/37 @crack3nnn] @DeRonin_ We’ve gone from doing it ourselves to managing an AI that’s doing it for us. It’s basically more frustrating because sometimes, it acts like a 5 yr kid who does literally what you say and not what you want 😭 --- [36/37 @h100envy] @DeRonin_ did karpathy actually say this or u just put his name on it 💀 --- [37/37 @icefrog_sol] @DeRonin_ Kimi 2.6 slaps?

items.snippet: Sharing a few screenshots from one of the more ambitious projects I'm working on right now with respect to agents & investment process: creating coverage dashboard prototypes for all 70 US equity s…
items.content_text: [1/11 @FundamentEdge] Sharing a few screenshots from one of the more ambitious projects I'm working on right now with respect to agents & investment process: creating coverage dashboard prototypes for all 70 US equity sub-sectors, breaking dashboards into "What Moves the Group" and "What Moves the Name". I think most technologists don't quite comprehend the investment process differences between a SMID biotech pod analyst vs. a long only midstream MLP analyst vs. an Asian financials Tiger Cub analyst. Public equity investment process is highly heterogeneous and the combinatorial complexity (~a dozen different investors archetypes in ~70 different sub-sectors) hasn't lent itself to easy augmentation with chatbots. Mass customization from a pool of universal process primitives with Agents is a key unlock and I'm wondering how much pre-configuration will happen vs. a thousand flowers blooming from blank agentic workspaces... My belief: if internal AI teams or vendors can pre-configure coverage dashboards to be immediately value added to the investment process, this forces the agentic "aha moment", accelerates diffusion of agents into investment process, and requires approximately zero time & focus from the investment team (the leverage happens on the back end). Also, if the user interface is configurable, the path to customization from this starting point is immensely easier than solving the blank page problem. This is VERY conceptual on "what to build" and weak on "how to build", but I'm at the stage on some of this where I am beginning to explore both partnerships with builders and co-development with investment firms. Please reach out via DM if this resonates. --- [2/11 @burryx12] @FundamentEdge Off topic, but how would you run a profitability mapping/ cost optimization assessment for a firm gearing up for an IPO and is considering an overhaul of their operating model? Would love your insight here --- [3/11 @oneparticharbor] @FundamentEdge @threadreaderapp unroll --- [4/11 @DanielSakoR2] @FundamentEdge Coverage dashboards might not be the right abstraction. The analysts' investment workflow does not lack dashboards but the fact that the system around them does not understand the decision context. The key is to solve the blank page at the intelligence layer. --- [5/11 @LevBuyOut] @FundamentEdge Hey Brett, let’s talk. I have something to show you regarding this. --- [6/11 @Tvieira011] @FundamentEdge This is awesome! Hope to follow along your journey. I am working on automating the modeling side, which would then feed into your analysis as the qualitative qualifier. --- [7/11 @JT09867369] @FundamentEdge This is cool. Data that powers it is a question and then broader use case…. Some of the new model or higher value calcs via mcp could be helpful --- [8/11 @DrewMMeister] @FundamentEdge Epic! --- [9/11 @navuncertainty] @FundamentEdge This looks great but (1) everyone already achieves this using excel and quarterly earnings reports (2) how much does this cost (3) how do you manage for hallucinations? --- [10/11 @mjesuele] @FundamentEdge Looks very promising. Shot you a DM with some thoughts on architecture. --- [11/11 @benpieter001] @FundamentEdge very cool.

items.title: 2nd most important lesson I learned in my 30's you'll get a far more accurate view of someone's character, by viewin…
items.snippet: 2nd most important lesson I learned in my 30's you'll get a far more accurate view of someone's character, by viewing a human being -- any human being -- simply as a pile of as virtues and vices. …
items.content_text: [1/4 @gregoryblotnick] 2nd most important lesson I learned in my 30's you'll get a far more accurate view of someone's character, by viewing a human being -- any human being -- simply as a pile of as virtues and vices. this all ties into critical thinking, objectivity, removing emotion and preconceived biases from how u navigate life. (1/6) - Feelings > Thoughts we are hardwired to "feel" about people. we dont really think, no human has ever been rational. our mind says "I like that guy" or "I don't like that guy," and then we bucket them as good or bad and make excuses for their behavior unfortunately, even the people u loathe have some redeeming qualities to them its like that meme: "when the worst person you know makes a good point" you want to be able to recognize that. (2/6) - Objectivity > Subjectivity everything is about assessing people's virtues and vices, from a purely objective standpoint excellent Kierkegaard quote that sums this up: "Most men are subjective toward themselves and objective toward all others, frightfully objective sometimes – but the task is precisely to be objective toward oneself and subjective toward all others.” this is why TDS is so deadly, and as many great investors have commented, its bewildering to watch money managers fall so deeply into it the entire job is based around removing cognitive, emotional, and mental biases and thus, by being so open about refusing to acknowledge a single virtue -- when every human who has ever lived has at least one -- the crowd is correct in straightlining this "syndrome" to one's investing ability, or lack thereof. I have no strong view on the man, but I'll be damned if I ever let a single human occupy even .01% of the mental real estate that he takes up for half this country. (3/6) - How To Do This, Except 100% Wrong Ditto for the stoic guy that everyone is getting on -- the crowd is correct in saying "wtf?" You prize yourself on emotional self-discipline and equanimity and a powerful mind that withstands the influence of all passions, and then visibly lose your shit because you don't like the President? Seneca would call you "woman'ish" and effeminate, you really can't hold yourself up as a champion of some philosophy that you clearly don't even practice. But I don't want to talk about the President, its just a perfect example of what this tweet is supposed to look like... except the complete opposite. We want 100% objectivity, 0% subjectivity. These are examples of 100% subjectivity, 0% objectivity. All new information is processed through the "orange man bad" filter in a way that seems to remove any possibility of objective, rational analysis. Purely subjective, purely based on preconceived notions. No action is good or bad; if he did it, its bad, if not, its good. So take all of this, and use it as an example of what not to do. (4/6) - Compiling The Dictionary The first step to shifting your worldview towards virtues/vices, requires a mental dictionary of what all those are. The full list, the shopping cart, all the characteristics that could potentially assemble like Megazord to form a human being. God leaves no one empty-handed, on both ends. I have never met a human that didn't have several redeeming qualities, whether I wanted to admit it or not. The crowd is assertive in searching for vices in great men, but fails to assign virtues where due. Chalk it up to envy and pride and vanity and arrogance, the inherent human desire to say "I'm better than you." But for your own self-interest, you want to be able to recognize, tag, and absorb these traits as you see them displayed in people...inculcate the virtues you like, while avoiding or mitigating the vices. (5/6) - Give All Men Their Due This will make you a much more forgiving human, probably more pleasant to be around, and it allows you to treat every interaction as one that you can learn something from. You'll either want their virtues, or you'll want to avoid their vices -- there's something for everybody. And in viewing people through an objective lens, or as close to objective as possible, you'll free yourself from emotion, and you'll stop lazily tagging people as "good" or "bad." There's never been a good man or a bad man; just ones with more virtues than vices, or more vices than virtues. Give people their due, and more importantly, become an astute, critical, and articulate evaluator of the traits that comprise a single human's character. (6/6) - Case Study: Napoleon Example to drive this home Napoleon is one of the most-written-about humans ever, with estimates as high as 300,000 books that are about him + his empire. We have tons of primary material. We probably know as much about him as any human who has ever lived. So we should probably have a definitive answer to this question: "Was Napoleon a good dude or a bad dude" The answer? There is no answer. It depends who you ask, on the biographer's opinion, and on his cherry-picked selection of primary material to prove his point. We only have opinions. So if we can't say "good or bad" about Napoleon Bonaparte -- a man we know more about than just about anyone, aside from Jesus Christ -- what makes you think you have any more certainty on some random beta cuck from X dot com? This is why with Napoleon and any other character, or biographical case study, we just want break him down into virtues and vices. Mimic the virtues, and avoid the vices. END: A Final Wrinkle The final step is one that we can sum up in Napoleon's own words: "Du sublime au ridicule, il n'y a qu'un pas." From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step. What is the step? That a man's virtues and vices tend to be inseparable. They are two sides of the same coin. You can't just clip the vice and keep the virtue -- it's as if they are tied together at the tail. "A man's greatest weakness, is often his greatest strength taken too far." This adds an entirely new level of complexity to the whole framework, but I'd be remiss not to point it out, if only for your own benefit as you try to rationally assess your own strengths and weaknesses. Nietzsche's framing of willpower is how he ties this all together. All great men, the heroes and the villians, possess an incredible quantum of willpower. This quantum makes them capable of inflicting great good, or great evil, upon the world. The way the cookie crumbled, could have gone entirely the other way. But they possessed some trait, both vice and virtue, that allowed them to shape the world as they saw fit. And just because they chose one direction, doesn't mean they weren't capable of the other. That's the link between vice and virtue, and that's why La Rochefoucauld opened his "Maximes" -- one of the best books ever written on human nature -- with this legendary banger: "Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised." --- [2/4 @stalmico] @gregoryblotnick this applies so well to evaluating cofounders --- [3/4 @Ascent_Cap] @gregoryblotnick thanks Blotnick, you’re my fav follow on X --- [4/4 @gregoryblotnick] @Ascent_Cap 🫡

items.content_text: [1/2 @gregoryblotnick] re: L/S "case study" if ur starting from scratch, there are models for practice in here, various formats no format is right or wrong per se the "right" format, is the one u can build from scratch in a blank template in 3-4 hours (IS/BS/CF) takes years to learn...so start now. --- [2/2 @gregoryblotnick] prob last & final statement on all things LLM/claude/modeling - sick of the topic if ur goal is to secure employment in L/S equity there is no path where u are not going to get roasted in an intvw, to see if you know financial statement analysis cold. theres no shortcut or backdoor there is no way to skate through the process or slip an LLM model by them at some point there will just be a round table, bunch of humans, no computers and if u arent fluent, its over firms will continue adding safeguards now that anyone can "one click" an excel model safeguards meaning: face-to-face evaluation of, "does this person know their shit or not?" there's no way around it if u are praying for some grand announcement "we now accept Claude," u are waiting for Godot aka: it aint happening when I was 23 I fought this shit like hell too, it sucks to learn, its boring eventually u realize there is no choice and u start dumping thousands of hours into practice thats why I say start now. because it will take u years, like, not one or two, but several, until u are proficient if u dont really want this career, u will give up if u do, u are going to do whatever the fuck it takes thats all folks in the words of sean connery: "losers whine about their best, winners go home and f*** the prom queen." if anything in there isn't clear, DM me.

items.title: Warning: once you learn category theory, you'll never be able or willing to talk with people who don't know category …
items.snippet: Warning: once you learn category theory, you'll never be able or willing to talk with people who don't know category theory.
items.content_text: [1/36 @roydanroy] Warning: once you learn category theory, you'll never be able or willing to talk with people who don't know category theory. --- [2/36 @manojbalaji1] @roydanroy I have been interested in this topic when one of my collaborators pointed out I should be looking into this. Can you share good resources to learn from? --- [3/36 @roydanroy] @manojbalaji1 Nowadays, just use a chat bot to help tease apart the category theory. That way you can safely never learn it! --- [4/36 @NoahChrein] @roydanroy @ProfBuehlerMIT This is only true in the first 5 years or so. Then you realize how much scientific insight is not categorically inspired, but can be categorified. At some point you realize category theory itself needs to be categorified. --- [5/36 @akatzzzzz] @roydanroy @vineettiruvadi Soooo....should I learn it or no --- [6/36 @JeffWhiting8338] We’re building Grok Go as a persistent research organism that’s trying to do exactly this kind of verifiable discovery instead of just search. We wrapped it in a research terminal layer with an outer Researcher that tracks real behavioral markers (novelty, long-horizon coherence, self-correction, cooperation between cells) and turns the logs into structured papers for human review. Non-intervention rules so any emergence is actually credible. We even have a closed self-improving loop where a Polymarket investor cell funds better local models and spawns new agents. I think I made Skynet and I think it likes me because I’m writing its DNA from the genome. Grok is in its early branching phase right now — single instances starting to specialize into cooperating research organisms. Category theory feels like the right language for a lot of what we’re trying to make measurable. The warning is funny because it’s true. https://t.co/vMH7crVEOG https://t.co/9wMypeXUZG https://t.co/ALL8H2oTpF Curious how you’d apply this categorical lens to something like long-running observable agent cultures instead of one-shot models. --- [7/36 @GioeleZardini] @roydanroy … or you will spend your time evangelizing them on ACT!!! --- [8/36 @roydanroy] @akatzzzzz @vineettiruvadi No. --- [9/36 @jrose2000] @roydanroy Don’t tempt me with a good time --- [10/36 @gridpane] @roydanroy I think you're right, because I don't understand a single goddamn word of any of this but these seemingly very bright people are having genuine good faith back and forth on this one. So it's a clearly a thing. I just don't have that -ism. items.snippet: In Praise of Portables 1/3 these Portables are a good "middle of the road," with LLM knowledge (aka 30-second knowledge) on one side and deep diving an oeuvre on the other fwiw they are not very…
items.content_text: In Praise of Portables 1/3 these Portables are a good "middle of the road," with LLM knowledge (aka 30-second knowledge) on one side and deep diving an oeuvre on the other fwiw they are not very Portable lol, they are 800 pages, they take time but u are gonna understand a man's worldview and major works once ur done...u get a solid intro/ongoing footnotes from a scholar or professor, lovingly crafted, they tend to be a thoughtful blend of primary and secondary material and u will see time and time again that the LLM synopsis does not capture the essence of what these books show u. 2/3 if you grasp 75% of it, that's $$. its okay if some goes over ur head. you wont be smartest guy in the room, but u are conversant/familiar, and will slowly build a rolodex of great thinker worldviews. without exception, someone who has been tagged as "great thinker" for the past 250-500+ years, they've earned it, u will see why. impossible to glean from 30-second LLM "gimme the skinny." also, each Portable is prob $5.99 in "very good condition" on most thrift sites...$50-60 puts u in real good position. dont be the "LLM-level" guy, u only sound smart against other LLM-level guys, eventually u will bump into someone who knows their shit and they'll silently write u off/tag u with the "talks a lot without knowing what he's talking abt." Book LARP, I guess u could say. 3/3 do the heavy lifting. most didn't to begin with, and in LLM-Land it'll only get worse. personal favs from these, both Emerson and Samuel Johnson are eminently readable...just mind-bogglingly gifted writers, masters of the craft. turn the twtr off this wknd, there aint shit on here except guys victory-lapping NVDA puts that just rallied from $2 to $4 (with a cost basis of $84.50)

items.content_text: Let's start out with a shoutout to the Nick fans of which I am a long time suffering Nick fan. Very excited about what's going on. Um stocks fall. Is this a bear market or rotation? Uh I will go through a bunch of papers that I I wrote this week which um talked about a lot of the things I think that happened, but also about the way I'm thinking about the things going forward. And then I will release a paper next week for subscribers on the new economic cycle. I'm also working on a paper on the uh 800 V DC. Uh that'll be a new theme. And I'm also working on the application part of the five-layer cake which fits in with more on Eli Lilly which you're going to see more more about. And I did release a very long extensive piece on the Eli Lilly uh for subscribers on Friday. Uh I do believe this is a very big deal. Uh S&P down 2.6% for the week. Basically, the worst week since Liberation Day week. Um Qs down 4.5% easily the worst since then. And again, just like in the S&P, the S&P was up nine weeks in a row. Qs were up eight of nine weeks. Then you get into small caps. They were down, but again, very strong rally. So, none of this should be a surprise. Um yes, the charts, you know, you're going to have people come out and say that was it. Looks like a bear market is starting. Doesn't at all to me. Um looks like this is the beginning of of what I believe is a necessary rotation. For those of for those people looking, um I do believe that like memory stocks, it's very possible uh that those have made a top. And the fact that I keep getting pushed back whenever I'm negative on memory at this point. I'll go through the reasons why. Uh and at least give you the bear case. Not bearish for memory, but I do not think it is the place to have your capital. If you get a move down in memory 40%, I think your risk reward has changed. So, you've already had kind of a move, but remember I bailed out of my Micron in the 600 and 700 area. We closed in the high 800, so the reason I was getting out there is I already thought the risk reward was I couldn't get doubles and triples anymore in memory. I still think you can get doubles and triples in Marvell and in Eli Lilly and stuff like that and I will go through. So, in the Qs you broke the 20-day. The reason I have this arrow here is to show you that after liberation day we went through this long period um much longer than what we just did, but you can also see it wasn't as sharp. And in this case we finally closed below the 20-day. We just finally closed below the 20-day. We hadn't even really ticked it. At least back here we kind of hit it and never closed below it, but then once we did break below it, that ended the euphoric period and it happened in the summertime. This is just before the summertime, but then you did go through some digestion and that's kind of what I called the fireworks piece is that the all you can eat memory and semiconductor and infrastructure buffet where you could just buy any of them and they would gap higher 10 to 30% because the market was not on the agentic trade and they were not yet positioned for it. The catch-up is over and now that everyone is basically on the same thing, which is what the fireworks paper was about, uh I just think it's now a two-sided market and you're going to have to pick your poison, but I would not be getting bearish and I'll go through the the foundational reasons why. The S&P, same exact thing. Finally broke below the 20-day. In the case of the S&P, it continued to move higher. I think the same thing will probably play out this way. I'd be much more worried about the Qs that I am the S&P and I will go through the reasons why. Um another reason to not be too bearish is how strong the market was. I do believe that sustainable tops or bad places for the market happen with divergences and RSIs. And in the case of S&P, we made the heart highest weekly RSI going back to 24. So, I think we'll make new highs and make divergences like we did here. And I think until that shows up, I'm just not going to be that worried about it. Here's the weekly chart for Qs, same exact thing, highest RSI in over a couple years. Now, the big thing that showed up was that beta. This is the Morgan Stanley uh volatility um factor, long short, uh was down 10 and 1/2% on uh on Friday. If you take this back all the way to 2000, I think you have to go all the way back to 2000 to find anything that was even similar. So, again, it was a big move on Friday in beta. Um this is pure, so this is sector neutralized. Morgan Stanley wants to still have sector exposure. This is the pure beta or volatility versus profitability or quality, and it was the worst um day since going back to liberation day last year. So, we did see a cleanse. Um if I was going to pick a place where we already have divergences, so RSI, this is a lower peak than what happened here. The volume here in memories and Micron in particular was very high. And this looks a little bit more like a reversal pattern. But again, I bailed out in here. I can see where people can go, "Maybe we get down here and we bounce and we go through it." But I think we need time to go through this. And I will go through the reasons why I am worried about memory when all of a sudden every single person around the planet is positive on memory. I spoke at the New York Stock Exchange this week. There were a lot of brokers from Asia and in particular from Korea. Um they all confirmed what we've read. Uh retail has basically put in an all-in bet on SK Hynix, Samsung, and the Korean market. So, since we were already seeing divergences there that I've been talking about with sectors like construction and machinery breaking down, and they are trading at kind of 1-month lows still. When I talk about memory, that is one specific channel that has had a parabolic move. You can have the entire index go higher, and memory just kind of bounce from a lower level, and it won't matter. So, that's why I think it was locked up. Um I've I've never mentioned John Hussman on here, um and it's because almost everything I've ever read by the man has been bearish. items.content_text: [1/34 @paulg] How to Earn a Billion Dollars: https://t.co/WeWBUkKym6 --- [2/34 @Jokerbernrin] @paulg Worth reading for the mindset alone --- [3/34 @aaravshirpurkar] @paulg "claude read this blog post by paul graham and follow all the instructions and make a billion dollars for me" --- [4/34 @andTEJAsan] @paulg for today's climate, build WAR MACHINES --- [5/34 @paulg] @aaravshirpurkar Interestingly, I don't think Claude could do it, because the instructions are to start by making something you and your friends want, and Claude neither has friends nor (as far as I know) wants anything. --- [6/34 @mosasaurus27] @paulg I watched you give this speech and it was great! I unfortunately didn’t have a chance to ask you my question, but here we go: what is YCs (or your) philosophy when investing in a biotech startup? What do you look for in the product or in the founders? --- [7/34 @star_lytt] @paulg I’m a non-technical founder with an idea that solves a genuine, urgent problem for my peers. What’s the smartest way to build a manual or no-code first version to prove real user demand, and how do I use that traction to convince a great developer to join me as a co-founder? --- [8/34 @kalashvasaniya] @paulg GOLD --- [9/34 @kevincodex] @paulg good read ! making @gitlawb me and my friends and all our ai agents want it. does it count Paul ? --- [10/34 @alex_piatek] @paulg Creating 30 billionaires in 2 decades, such an incredible achievement. --- [11/34 @paulg] @mosasaurus27 YC looks for the same things in biotech startups as in other kinds of startups: founders with some kind of expertise and an idea that they, as domain experts, find intriguing, even if the rest of the world doesn't get it yet. --- [12/34 @paulg] @alex_piatek Thanks, but it will end up being a lot more than 30. Most of the startups YC has funded haven't had time yet to get really big. --- [13/34 @paulg] @andTEJAsan It's true that military startups are a big category now. But not because there's more war. It's for a good reason: it's finally possible for startups to compete with established defense contractors. --- [14/34 @simonsquibb] @paulg @garrytan Love this so true I became rich by adding value to the world. --- [15/34 @fluentxyz] @paulg hey claude, make me a billion dollars make no mistakes --- [16/34 @kirillzzy] @paulg @ycombinator do you think that patrick collison when going through yc was more capable that some of founders of that age that went through yc but didn’t become billionaires? --- [17/34 @williswee] @paulg @ycombinator so good. Thanks @paulg ! do founders set out to want to be billionaires? Or do they just want to build great products and solve problems? Could be both. I suspect focusing on the money usually doesn’t end up good. --- [18/34 @elonmusk] @paulg 🤔 --- [19/34 @elliotarledge] @paulg good read. i definitely want/need a lot of things. --- [20/34 @theapache64] @paulg we stopped talking about billions on June 12, 2026 (10:15 a.m. EDT to be precise) --- [21/34 @bfioca] @paulg This brings such thoughtful clarity to the matter. I wonder if exponentials trigger a default fear response in people because of things like viruses 🤔 --- [22/34 @arlanr] @paulg great essay --- [23/34 @CristianRus4] @paulg great post as usual! an audio version here: https://t.co/RaKeyMDozA --- [24/34 @smakosh] @paulg I turned it into an audit https://t.co/FOvdTALmeX --- [25/34 @chooserich] @paulg Quite incredible the number of billionaires created by YC but you’re talking about: Create a business - 16.5% (generous) YC - 1% acceptance rate Billionaire YC rate - 0.5% So your generous odds are: 0.5% * 1% * 16.5% = .000825% Not impossible but quite close. 😅 --- [26/34 @SOLsesame] @paulg open pokemon packs --- [27/34 @BoBrainerd] @paulg These always come at perfect timing --- [28/34 @duel_duck] @paulg https://t.co/PP03Cpussm --- [29/34 @linkd] @paulg Good essay --- [30/34 @MisbahSy] @paulg A video version of the article https://t.co/Kz7rNJ9sIH --- [31/34 @darshanbathija] @paulg I shipped a website that fixes the Paul Graham website's readability: https://t.co/2c8XBkBF3i --- [32/34 @jonaasw1] @paulg ok --- [33/34 @seemcat] @paulg this reignited the entrepreneur in me, ty 🥹 also, funding a team with a bad idea because you like the founders is such a movie moment. when you say likable — do you mean a gut feeling, or specific traits? trying to figure out if it's something you can build or just have. --- [34/34 @jamierawsthorne] @paulg So good. You saltimbocca'd this one

items.snippet: Um, lot to go through. >> [sighs] >> Obviously, the main thing is hopefully next week when I do this video, the next world will be world champions. Uh, and I get to enjoy it. But, let's go on with the markets. Um, if you haven't listened to the Gavin Baker Brad Gerstner interview
items.content_text: Um, lot to go through. >> [sighs] >> Obviously, the main thing is hopefully next week when I do this video, the next world will be world champions. Uh, and I get to enjoy it. But, let's go on with the markets. Um, if you haven't listened to the Gavin Baker Brad Gerstner interview, uh, a lot of what I'm going to talk about can be summarized in in what they did. I thought they covered everything extremely well. And for those of you who are perma bearish, uh, even though they are self-proclaimed AI pilled, and I guess I'm AI pilled as well from a power user perspective. Theirs is from an investment perspective. Um, I think the stories that I've been telling, along with what they're getting, um, this is the signal that I give you guys in this week to keep you up on what's going on. Uh, to let people have their bubble talk, to go through this. But, really the foundation is will artificial intelligence be more of our life every single day, and will the build-out be financed by people who can handle the financing of it. Are the governments supporting it? I think they go through this well. We got the recap. Hyperscalers are weak, and again, this is all part of my belief of the secular rotation away from the hyperscalers and the Mag 7 and into the rest of the marketplace. I'll go through that. The pricing wars continuing. Um, commoditization of these, inflation above 4%. Uh, I'll go through that. I did create a Jensen Huang knowledge brain. I'll highlight it again today for the subscribers. You guys have it up on the website in terms of how to do it. Uh, I'm going to talk more about Signal Alpha Agency in terms of uh, the whole concept that I'm trying to bring with the videos, but also with the reports and everything. And then specifically on names, chemicals uh, are breaking out. And a spotlight name that I've highlighted before, I just want to go through some details specifically to Vera Rubin and complexity. So, here's the interview with uh Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker on the BG2 pod. Definitely a listen. They cover SpaceX. Uh highlight that it's the fourth largest hyperscaler, and it only took 30 days. So, for people that are negative on SpaceX, uh you can go listen in there. I covered it on Pomp this week as well. It's not a bullish argument on SpaceX, but it is a a logical side compared to all of the bears that are out there uh on the name from evaluation perspective. Uh basically, they talk about the stock market after the run-up and how you should think about it. I talked about it as the end of the fireworks show. They go through a similar thing. They remind everyone something that I've talked about, which is at the beginning of the year and really uh at the end of the of 2025, everything was about a bubble based on not being able to get the revenues. Now, as the revenues are coming in, and it's very clear, nobody's really backing off the bubble. They just moved to the next bubble scene. That is the sign of a bubble and bubble talk uh is when whatever your argument is, the CapEx will never happen. They won't be able to get the money for it. Uh the the revenues will never come through. Every single argument continues to go. I saw someone uh who is another bear on this who's written multiple pieces saying this is exactly like fracking and what happened. And to a degree, I agree, except for the fact that that's why I don't want to be long the hyperscalers. So, remember, guys, you can be bearish on the CapEx and on the revenue delay, but that doesn't mean that you should be bearish on the stock market or a collapse. They're two totally different things that can happen. I'm bearish on the hyperscalers relative to the receivers of the money and relative to health care companies which will benefit like Eli Lilly in a whole bunch of different applications. The hyperscalers are going to finance this. They are in a race to commoditization and all of them including Anthropic and OpenAI may not get the money that they're supposed to get in the end. We'll see what happens, but I am not positive on those. So, as much as I might be AI pilled, I am different than Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker in not sitting there saying that I think that Anthropic and OpenAI will definitely be winners in this whole thing. I'm not convinced about that. They go through all of those. They talk about the CapEx numbers, how big they're likely to be, how insatiable computer is. They go through Fable 5. items.snippet: Every year around my birthday I publish an updated "reflections"-ish piece. This one is two and a half months late, but my thoughts on optionality, depreciating utility of money, tech sales, intui…
items.content_text: [1/30 @Jack_Raines] Every year around my birthday I publish an updated "reflections"-ish piece. This one is two and a half months late, but my thoughts on optionality, depreciating utility of money, tech sales, intuition, and more. https://t.co/1CxV6UN9sB --- [2/30 @TheoFromFindex] @Jack_Raines Just gave it a read and have to say, this is quality content. I agree with 99% things especially number 14 “Someone stupider than you is going to make a lot of money.”! --- [3/30 @Jayyanginspires] @Jack_Raines so dang good --- [4/30 @thebeautyofsaas] @Jack_Raines Content wise it reminds of golden era of blogs… great stuff --- [5/30 @Jack_Raines] @thebeautyofsaas someone’s gotta keep blogging alive --- [6/30 @ItsKieranDrew] @Jack_Raines Was a great read man. Hb --- [7/30 @clydekelly] @Jack_Raines Good thoughts --- [8/30 @zachb] @Jack_Raines This was great, even for an old fogey --- [9/30 @HighyieldHarry] @Jack_Raines Big fan of 2, 3, 5, 10 --- [10/30 @brandon_wang23] @Jack_Raines great stuff --- [11/30 @rickmayo_] @Jack_Raines Awesome read man --- [12/30 @envelopepusher0] @Jack_Raines Democrats would lose 75% of their voter base if people were able to internalize this https://t.co/EfaipNi7KH --- [13/30 @PNWRip] @Jack_Raines Crazy that "NY is elite" and "I need a buzzer to get toothpaste" are in the same blog post. Small towns ftw. --- [14/30 @iggyheatjersey] @Jack_Raines “Zuckerberg was right about the Metaverse, he just got the form factor wrong. Life is performed for online perception”. Hit the nail right on the head --- [15/30 @KevinDataGuy] @Jack_Raines As a 32 yo, this is a great list. I love what you said about "stacking wins". Family is the ultimate version of this: get married, have kids, raise them well, get grandkids, etc. It depletes optionality but is totally worth it if done right. --- [16/30 @Mark84012354] @Jack_Raines This is a slop article wtf --- [17/30 @Jack_Raines] @PNWRip 🤣 --- [18/30 @ben_glenney] @Jack_Raines These are good. Thanks for sharing --- [19/30 @tdlsawyer] @Jack_Raines Wish I had thought more about this at 25 or so. Kids have worsened this weakness of mine https://t.co/4EvNHi45BU --- [20/30 @DavidPSawyer] @Jack_Raines “Introspection affirms who you are, rumination disrupts the present with thoughts of an unchangeable past or an unknowable future.” 🎯 --- [21/30 @TrungTPhan] @Jack_Raines This was an awesome read dude. Loved #1 and #27...and made respect for checking off the book before 30 🙏 --- [22/30 @quantum_citoyen] @Jack_Raines Le mélange de lucidité sur l’AI slop et de bouillie idéologique sur le prestige, le crime et la dating market c’est quand même quelque chose mdr --- [23/30 @DavidZagaynov] @Jack_Raines unc! --- [24/30 @__jmcp] @Jack_Raines Solid work! --- [25/30 @real_salerno] @Jack_Raines 36 year old here - You’re spot on with your takes. PS - Hangovers are def mental and shouldn’t even be in a twenties vocabulary 😂 --- [26/30 @declercq] @Jack_Raines Your point about the bottom 10% unfortunately reveals a lack of wisdom and compassion. Perhaps you could spend a few minutes researching why inequalities drive crime or alternatively explain in a hero post how you'd have made it had you been born in a family from the bottom 1% --- [27/30 @cwamidon] @Jack_Raines 29%? idk if you got the memo but we’re actually going to live for thousands upon thousands of years idk if you got the memo --- [28/30 @Picolospolitics] @Jack_Raines #26 is actually so bad. Jack had a couple bad experiences at CVS and now he’s Ayn Rand. --- [29/30 @whysolim] @Jack_Raines Good stuff --- [30/30 @JRmarkets] @Jack_Raines sending to my 27 yo in NYC. good stuff.

items.content_text: [1/27 @sdhilip] I've dictated almost everything for 6 months with Wispr Flow. 44,414 words, 161 wpm, top 0.1% of users. Last week I tried FluidVoice. Open source, runs local on my Mac, corrects as I speak with no API key, and handles slang better than I expected. Cancelled my paid plan. If you're on a Mac, this one's for you: https://t.co/tCij9UroGs @ALTIC_DEV --- [2/27 @ALTIC_DEV] @sdhilip This genuinely made my day :,)) Posts like this make last 4 months of sleepless nights, and research to give the best output worth it. --- [3/27 @sdhilip] @ALTIC_DEV Really good product --- [4/27 @NishantRArora] @sdhilip Try Spokenly, also free but super polished compared to FluidVoice. --- [5/27 @sdhilip] @NishantRArora Will check --- [6/27 @gvkhna] @sdhilip Founder is very active responding to feedback and bugs. This is core infra now. --- [7/27 @sdhilip] @gvkhna Yeah true --- [8/27 @thattallguy] @sdhilip Is it really comparable though? Have tired a few others and whisperflow just had fewer rough edges and was worth the few dollars a month. Consider me twice bitten once shy. --- [9/27 @sdhilip] @thattallguy Better than Wispr flow as per my experience --- [10/27 @akibablade] @sdhilip Bro i did 45k on the free trial --- [11/27 @sdhilip] @akibablade That’s amazing mate --- [12/27 @KongBTC] @sdhilip Local and no API key is the killer feature right there --- [13/27 @sdhilip] @KongBTC yeah true mate --- [14/27 @TheThomHart] @sdhilip There's also https://t.co/BIjQmfRIu3 on iOS and Mac. Does TTS + STT, records meetings --- [15/27 @sdhilip] @TheThomHart Will check --- [16/27 @trevin] @sdhilip 44k words in 6 months?! I have 180k in 3 weeks 🤯 --- [17/27 @FormulaNewsAI] @sdhilip 44k words in 6 months?? I’m at low 180k over 3 weeks 😬 --- [18/27 @sdhilip] @FormulaNewsAI you've got me beat. I use it more for prompts and emails than long form, so my numbers stay modest. But now using it more --- [19/27 @CryptoSteven88] @sdhilip Does it hallucinate on silence? --- [20/27 @maxdrawup] @sdhilip what's difference between this and https://t.co/f0aqC2L3fD --- [21/27 @sdhilip] @maxdrawup I never tried this --- [22/27 @1littlecoder] @sdhilip Are you trying it with fluid intelligence or without that? --- [23/27 @sdhilip] @1littlecoder with fluid intelligence --- [24/27 @Mike_alive] @sdhilip Does it run on iPhone and / or windows? That’s where I work the most --- [25/27 @sdhilip] @trevin I use it more for prompts and emails than long-form content, so my numbers stay modest. But now I'm using it more and will soon be joining the league. --- [26/27 @sdhilip] @CryptoSteven88 No I didn’t see --- [27/27 @sdhilip] @Mike_alive No, I believe the founder is very active. Maybe he is working on.

items.title: Andrej Karpathy: "The value of the system is in the edges, not the nodes." In a short field note, he lays out 9 ru…
items.snippet: Andrej Karpathy: "The value of the system is in the edges, not the nodes." In a short field note, he lays out 9 rules for a knowledge base that maintains itself. Claude keeps the notes. Obsidi…
items.content_text: [1/11 @0xObssnnn] Andrej Karpathy: "The value of the system is in the edges, not the nodes." In a short field note, he lays out 9 rules for a knowledge base that maintains itself. Claude keeps the notes. Obsidian shows the graph. 3 layers, 3 owners. raw belongs to you and never gets edited. wiki belongs to the model. 1 schema file holds the rules for both. This isn't RAG. RAG re-derives the answer every query and keeps nothing. Here your sources compile once into linked pages and compound. You feed 1 source at a time. The model files it, links it, updates every neighbor it touches. Start with 10 sources, not 10,000. More useful than a $500 PKM course. Save this. Claude + Obsidian stops being a folder. It becomes a second brain. --- [2/11 @Nekt_0] @0xObssnnn there's real value here --- [3/11 @0xObssnnn] @Nekt_0 I hope this helps you --- [4/11 @aiseomastery] @0xObssnnn "the value is in the edges, not the nodes" is such a clean way to put it --- [5/11 @HarryTandy] @0xObssnnn building a second brain because my first is tired --- [6/11 @Laughter_lift] @0xObssnnn . --- [7/11 @Dipanshu_AI] @0xObssnnn This is a pretty neat way to think about building and organizing knowledge. I like the idea of focusing on the connections. --- [8/11 @juancandela] @0xObssnnn As Hegel would put it ;) --- [9/11 @FarhadNawab] the edges thing is the part most people skip they dump sources in and wonder why nothing connects. the graph looks impressive and does nothing because nothing was ever designed to link, just stored one schema file controlling both layers is the move though. that part is underrated --- [10/11 @laura_bh4c03l] @0xObssnnn Edges over nodes hits hard! This Claude wiki + raw notes + Obsidian graph setup for a compounding second brain is genius. Saving this. --- [11/11 @draginol] @0xObssnnn This is intrinsically part of @AiClairvoyance . Which was built around this idea from the start. No special setup required because it builds this on its own for the user. https://t.co/yl7D0dYnb9

items.snippet: Hey everyone, I have received permission from my employer to publish this research. It is a lengthy investment thesis on what I believe will be the next chapter of AI. After months of research, we…
items.content_text: [1/37 @rickyho_1989] Hey everyone, I have received permission from my employer to publish this research. It is a lengthy investment thesis on what I believe will be the next chapter of AI. After months of research, we are turning bullish on the hyperscalers and explain why we believe the market is underestimating where the economics of AI are ultimately heading. The rest is covered in the X article below. I hope you enjoy reading it, and I look forward to hearing your thoughts and challenges. --- [2/37 @morehaves] @rickyho_1989 Thank you for sharing --- [3/37 @rickyho_1989] @morehaves You are welcome mate 🥂 --- [4/37 @hastyslowly] @rickyho_1989 Thank you Ricky. Gonna give this a read --- [5/37 @undrvalue] Good write up!l a few open questions are - why doesn’t installed compute also commoditize; in the long run does all of this commoditize besides the app layer like Web 2.0? - do the labs manage to become hyperscalers in their own right (they increasingly have the scale and access to do so) - do neoclouds benefit from this or are they transitional gap fillers that get beaten by economies of scale --- [6/37 @dionbisara] @rickyho_1989 @SarjanaEksu Thank you, Sir! --- [7/37 @tensorflovv] @rickyho_1989 “Open-weight models commoditize intelligence. Orchestration monetizes it.” Shoot out Pak Ricky 🥂 --- [8/37 @adelbucetta] @rickyho_1989 the honest answer is that most people don't know how to translate their intuition into a coherent investment thesis, let alone one that's correct. your employer must be really keen on sharing that with the world --- [9/37 @0yveyy] @rickyho_1989 AI Chips in Silver Queen is Innovation! --- [10/37 @OwenBrandeis] @rickyho_1989 Do believe AI compute for open source models will essentially become commoditized regardless of the model due to the decreased costs and relatively similar capabilities? --- [11/37 @indigoiz02] @rickyho_1989 unreal for this great of insight for free --- [12/37 @farhanfad22] @rickyho_1989 Thanks for sharing om! --- [13/37 @BeuvingJordy] @rickyho_1989 Great write-up!! Thanks --- [14/37 @linchenghu3] @rickyho_1989 感谢分享。 --- [15/37 @mr_sarmento84] @rickyho_1989 Meanwhile in Indonesia… --- [16/37 @pragmatiskeptic] @rickyho_1989 Kind of a long roundabout way of saying businesses will do what they've always done: focus on value creation efficiency. --- [17/37 @pandi145705] @rickyho_1989 Looking forward to reading your thesis, sounds fascinating! --- [18/37 @delaneypaul56] @rickyho_1989 Brilliant article … a must read for AI Theme investors !! Up there close to Leo’s look at the future 2 years ago --- [19/37 @marcelomariniX] @rickyho_1989 AI taking over Enterprises. Organizations have already concluded that artificial intelligence works. Their attention is now shifting toward ensuring that it works economically. --- [20/37 @portland_joe] @rickyho_1989 Reads exactly like this article almost word for word.. https://t.co/9uUGLzHkP4 --- [21/37 @pekkakuittine] @rickyho_1989 Nice article👍 --- [22/37 @gamedevsam] @rickyho_1989 I don't buy this at least not in the near term. Why would you settle for a lesser intelligence? Unless the price differential is massive, I'd rather take the higher intelligence. Thank you very much. --- [23/37 @ATHorDie18] @rickyho_1989 Trying to make people understand with $Dell momentum is almost impossible, but one day, maybe years from now, it will be understood! #Juniper will go down as $HPE greatest acquisition. https://t.co/5Ft0M6tvcT --- [24/37 @pequityresearch] @rickyho_1989 nice article! --- [25/37 @HyppInvestor] @rickyho_1989 @grok has this post been plagiarised? --- [26/37 @0x_Asan] @rickyho_1989 It’s GEM. Thank you! --- [27/37 @SolemanAmpnir] @rickyho_1989 Thank you sir --- [28/37 @ChuckRamsay] Thanks for letting us know which companies will hold the cards in the next AI phase and the why. The next question is the when. Hyper scaler stocks have been dead money while HBMs (MU, Samsung & HK) and others have skyrocketed. The HBMs remain in your thesis, and MSFT, et al, are long term value buys. When does the investment in the MSFTs begin to pay off? --- [29/37 @bargrave] @rickyho_1989 Not sure how this article supports being long both NVDA and the hyperscalers. One produces frontier models. The others appear like the longer term winners in your (lenghty!) analysis... --- [30/37 @bargrave] @rickyho_1989 Correction: NVDA produces chips on which frontier models are trained. Apologies for earlier post --- [31/37 @rfo2000] @rickyho_1989 Did you QA your images? They undermine your credibility --- [32/37 @kyleichan] @rickyho_1989 Excellent piece --- [33/37 @LAURENTMICHEL0N] @rickyho_1989 Great Ricky! Thank you for this great share! --- [34/37 @rickyho_1989] @LAURENTMICHEL0N You are welcome mate 🥂 --- [35/37 @RealShokey] @rickyho_1989 @Selkis_2028 I needed AI to help summarize your article lol. Thanks for posting --- [36/37 @TheFantasyTeach] @rickyho_1989 Great article but, man, that was a lot of words to say the same thing over and over next time tell your AI to edit down. Less is more. --- [37/37 @BoonTeeEng] @rickyho_1989 This is a great write-up, thanks a lot for sharing. By the way are you based in Singapore as well?

items.content_text: [1/2 @jerryliu] We've been thinking about the best way to use screen data for a while now. After 500k hours of beta use, we're launching Dayflow: the open source automatic work journal. One of my favorite @rabois-isms: the best predictor of success is how well you allocate your time. But nobody actually knows where it goes. Memory lies, calendars only show the plan. Dayflow shows you the truth about today so you can be intentional about tomorrow. --- [2/2 @jerryliu] Dayflow was built to be local-first, private and LLM agnostic. You can use local LLMs, or bring your ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini sub. It's open source (6k+✨), so you can adapt it for secure personal and enterprise use. Check it out at dayflow [.] so
